title: From the Great Sphinx’s Raw Materials, a New Crocodile Species Surfaces - Nautilus
gist: Researchers from the U.K., Sweden, Germany and Egypt reclassified a fossil gavial from Egypt's Mokattam Formation as a new species, Herugavialis cairensis, after CT scans revealed skull differences from Tomistoma cairense. The rock unit is the same Tethys Sea limestone from which the Great Sphinx was carved.

themes.theme: New gavial species from Mokattam Formation

insights.claim: A new fish-eating crocodile species, Herugavialis cairensis, has been described from fossils in the Mokattam Formation east of Cairo, the same ancient Tethys Sea limestone the Great Sphinx was carved from.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Illustrates how re-examination of existing museum material continues to generate new scientific findings.
insights.quote: That same material—from the Mokattam Formation east of Cairo—has now yielded a new species of crocodile: Herugavialis cairensis.

insights.claim: The study describing Herugavialis cairensis was published in Royal Society Open Science by a multinational team from the U.K., Sweden, Germany and Egypt, led by University College London paleobiologist Paul Burke.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shows cross-border collaboration as the norm in Egyptian paleontology research.

insights.claim: The species was named after the Egyptian god Heru because its fossil skull lacks the snout tip, echoing the Great Sphinx's famously missing nose.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Cultural branding of discoveries helps science communication and public attention.

insights.claim: Fossil bones now assigned to Herugavialis cairensis were previously identified as another ancient Egyptian gavial, Tomistoma cairense, until CT scanning of the skull revealed differences warranting a new species.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Imaging technology applied to old specimens is a cheap engine of taxonomic revision.
insights.quote: But the study authors got a deeper look at the skull by CT-scanning it and found differences that warranted the new species classification.
